newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada markets shrug off election call.
newsitem.headline: Canada markets shrug off election call.

text.p: Canadian markets on Monday shrugged off the launch of Canada's election campaign, preoccupied instead with whether the U.S. Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again next month.
The Canadian dollar, bond and stock markets all edged lower after Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien's widely expected call on Sunday for a June 2 election.

"I don't really think this is a market that's going to pay a lot of attention, at least initially, to the Canadian federal election," said Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce foreign exchange specialist Reid Farrill.

"The market is assuming it will be a Liberal (Party) win and until it has reason to believe otherwise, interest rates are going to continue to key off developments south of the border and what happens to the exchange rate," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Canada Ltd.
An Angus Reid/Southam News poll released on Saturday showed support for Chretien's Liberals rose one point since late March to 42 percent of the decided vote, 24 points ahead of their nearest rival.

The Canadian dollar fell to C$1.3981 (US71.53 cents) from Friday's close of C$1.3970 (US71.58 cents), while Canada's 30-year government bond fell nearly half a point to yield 7.38 percent, up from 7.34 percent on Friday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Toronto stocks also fell, with the Toronto Stock Exchange index of 300 shares off 8.81 at 5,826.50 in afternoon trading.

The Canadian dollar had slipped as low as $C1.4000 at midday (US71.42 cents) on comments by Chretien on Monday that his government would reverse planned spending cuts because the government was ahead of schedule on deficit fighting.
"I think that turned the market a little negative," one trader said.
Canadian Imperial Bank's Farrill said the currency market would be awaiting U.S. economic data expected this week.

The expected U.S. employment cost, gross domestic product and payroll employment data could be an indicator of whether the Fed, the U.S. central bank, would raise rates when its policy-makers next meet on May 20.
"We don't like what's coming, so we're going south," Maison Placements Canada trader Joe Ismail said of the Canadian stock market's expectations.
The Fed on March 25 raised the federal funds rate, a key short-term rate that U.S. banks charge each other for overnight loans, a quarter point to to 5.5 percent.

Some economists said Canadian financial markets could be in a tough bind if the Fed raises short-term rates again in May. That could push the Canadian dollar sharply lower, below its two-year low of about C$1.4050 (US71.17 cents) and catching the Bank of Canada in a political trap.

"This is not an independent central bank," said Nesbitt Burns chief economist Sherry Cooper. "It's going to be a tough ride for them to raise interest rates in the midst of an election campaign that could well focus on the issue of jobs and the high unemployment rate in Canada."
